facts.text: Peatlands cover at least 3 percent of the world's land surface and are found in almost every country.
Peat forms where the ground stays waterlogged all year: the water slows the decay of dead plants, so they build up as peat.
In water-saturated peat, lack of oxygen limits decay; such peat is more than 95 percent water.
European peat is commonly said to build up by about 0.1 cm (1 millimeter) a year; a study of 28 sites found an average of 0.118 cm a year, ranging from 0.005 to 0.448 cm.
Peat soils hold more than 600 gigatonnes of carbon, up to 44 percent of all soil carbon, which is more carbon than all other kinds of vegetation combined.
When peat is drained, oxygen enters the soil and the peat breaks down, releasing carbon dioxide; drainage also raises the risk of fire.
Drained peat sinks: in the tropics by about 1 meter in the first year, then by 3 to 5 centimeters a year (1 to 2 centimeters a year in temperate regions).
Peat fires are very hard to put out: they can smolder for weeks or even months at and below the surface, survive days of rain or a cover of snow, and are finally stopped by a rising water table.
During Indonesia's 1997–98 drought, most fires were in peatlands disturbed by logging and drainage, while undisturbed peat swamp forest stayed at low risk of fire.
Between June and October 2015, about 2.6 million hectares of land burned in Indonesia, four and a half times the size of Bali.
Most of the 2015 fires, more than 100,000 of them, were set by people to clear land for farming, and drought linked to El Niño helped them spread.
About 33 percent of the land that burned in Indonesia in 2015 was peatland.
Derived: about two-thirds (67 percent) of the land that burned in Indonesia in 2015 was not peatland.
Smoke from the 2015 fires disrupted transport and trade, closed schools, and caused more than 500,000 cases of acute respiratory infection.
The 2015 fires cost Indonesia an estimated US$16.1 billion, about 1.9 percent of its GDP that year.
Carbon released by forest fires is usually taken back up as the forest grows again, but peat fires burn carbon stored over thousands of years that cannot be replaced.
Dry peat catches fire quickly and is difficult to put out.
Damaged peatlands cover only 0.3 percent of the world's land but produce almost 5 percent of human-caused carbon dioxide emissions.
Drained peatlands release an estimated 1.9 gigatonnes of CO2 equivalent a year, about 5 percent of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.
The 2015 fires in Indonesia's peat swamp forests released nearly 16 million tonnes of CO2 a day.

notes: 主題提示的「比全世界森林存的更多」以 IUCN 的說法「比其他所有植被加起來還多的碳」為準（UNEP 頁面在本環境無法讀取，不引用）。
